Neurology · published research

Stroke (acute)

Large acute-stroke trials found no clear improvement in 90-day functional outcome with the studied transcranial laser protocol, and NEST-3 stopped for futility. Some separate studies concern subacute or chronic recovery and should not be read as acute-stroke evidence.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Large acute-stroke trials found no clear improvement in 90-day functional outcome with the studied transcranial laser protocol, and NEST-3 stopped for futility. Some separate studies concern subacute or chronic recovery and should not be read as acute-stroke evidence.

Summary of the Evidence

The mapped clinical, preclinical and intravascular-stroke categories contain 71 database records, representing 71 unique titles. The set includes 15 unique human research titles, 38 animal publications, nine in-vitro or ex-vivo publications, 12 reviews, one meta-analysis, one protocol, one editorial and one other record. One human publication also includes laboratory work, so method counts overlap. Human reports include nine randomized publications, two other controlled or non-randomized reports, three case reports and one case series. Several randomized articles report the NeuroThera NEST program or related analyses and are not nine independent acute trials.

Human and clinical evidence

The acute-stroke evidence is dominated by the NEST program of single-session transcranial laser treatment. NEST-1 reported an initial favorable signal (Lampl et al. 2007), but the larger NEST-2 trial showed safety without meeting its prespecified efficacy threshold (Zivin et al. 2009). NEST-3 stopped after a futility analysis of 566 completed patients found no difference in the primary functional outcome (Hacke et al. 2014). A 2025 Cochrane review included four randomized acute-stroke trials and concluded that current evidence shows no clear benefit or harm, with little or no difference in unfavorable functional outcome (He et al. 2025). Other records address subacute or chronic rehabilitation, post-stroke cognition, intravenous laser irradiation or PBM combined with magnetic fields; they test different stages and routes and are not direct tests of acute reperfusion treatment.

Animal evidence

Thirty-eight animal publications include mouse, rat and rabbit models of cerebral ischemia. Many report changes in tissue injury, blood flow or behavior, but treatment timing, lesion model and exposure vary. Animal findings do not override neutral large human trials.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Nine laboratory publications include eight in-vitro and one ex-vivo study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The NEST acute protocol used transcranial near-infrared laser treatment around 808 nm, delivered once during the early period after stroke. Other records include red-light intravenous irradiation and later-stage rehabilitation protocols. These routes, treatment windows and target outcomes are not interchangeable. Dose, stroke severity and onset-to-treatment time matter for interpreting the acute trials.

Interpretation

The evidence does not support a clear 90-day functional benefit for the studied acute transcranial laser protocol. Large neutral trials and the pooled review outweigh favorable findings from early small studies. Later-stage rehabilitation and different light-delivery methods remain separate research questions rather than evidence that acute-stroke treatment is effective.

Evidence strength in source summaryModerate for no clear 90-day functional benefit with the studied single-session protocol Low for other protocols or treatment windows
Publications and records71 database records and 71 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several large sham-controlled acute-stroke trials and a recent Cochrane review do not show a clear functional benefit, and the phase III NEST-3 trial stopped for futility. The many stroke-category publications include repeated trial reports and studies of later recovery or intravenous treatment. Further work should test a clearly justified alternative protocol and keep acute outcomes separate from rehabilitation findings.
